questions.question: When riding in a group, where should inexperienced riders position themselves?

options.text: Just behind the leader.
In front of the group.
At the rear of the group.
Beside the leader.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This way, more experienced riders behind them can watch and help them.

questions.question: What is the minimum following distance when riding at night?

options.text: Two seconds.
Three seconds.
Four seconds.
Five seconds.

questions.correctAnswerText: Three seconds.
questions.explanation: At night, visibility is poor. You need at least three seconds of following distance. This gives you more time to see if the vehicle ahead stops and to brake safely.

questions.question: What should you do when going through a curve?

options.text: Always stay in the same portion of the lane throughout the entire curve.
Always stay in the left portion of the lane throughout the entire curve.
Always stay in the right portion of the lane throughout the entire curve.
Remember that the best path may not follow the curve of the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: Remember that the best path may not follow the curve of the road.
questions.explanation: Road and traffic conditions can change. Be ready to change your lane position. The best path through a curve does not always follow the road's curve.

questions.question: On a slippery surface, what should you NOT do?

options.text: Reduce your speed.
Avoid making sudden moves.
Use only the front brake when slowing or stopping.
Use both brakes when slowing or stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use only the front brake when slowing or stopping.
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, use both brakes, slow down, and avoid sudden moves. Watch for oil, dirt, gravel, shadows, and bridges—these are extra slippery.

questions.question: If a driver is following you too closely, what should you do?

options.text: Flash your brake light before you slow to warn the other driver.
Accelerate.
Pull over to the side of the road.
Slow down.

questions.correctAnswerText: Flash your brake light before you slow to warn the other driver.
questions.explanation: Flash your brake light before slowing down. This warns the tailgater that you are slowing and helps them see hazards ahead.

questions.question: How does motorcycle stopping distance compare to car stopping distance?

options.text: Cars need much longer to stop.
Cars need a little longer to stop.
Motorcycles need longer to stop.
Both motorcycles and cars take about the same amount of time to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: Both motorcycles and cars take about the same amount of time to stop.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles and cars stop in about the same distance under normal conditions. However, wet pavement makes stopping much harder for motorcycles.

questions.question: How should you cross tracks that run parallel to your lane?

options.text: Edge gradually across the tracks.
Cross the tracks at a 90-degree angle.
Wait for the tracks to end.
Move away from the tracks, turn, and cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees.

questions.correctAnswerText: Move away from the tracks, turn, and cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees.
questions.explanation: To safely cross railroad tracks, trolley tracks, or ruts, move to a position where you can cross at least 45 degrees. Make a quick, sharp turn. If you try to edge across slowly, the tracks can catch your tires and throw you off balance.

questions.question: When riding through a turn, where should you look?

options.text: Turn your head and shoulders to look through turns.
Keep your arms straight.
Keep your knees away from the gas tank.
Turn just your head and eyes to look through turns.

questions.correctAnswerText: Turn just your head and eyes to look through turns.
questions.explanation: Look through the turn to where you want to go. Turn only your head and eyes, not your shoulders. Keep your eyes level with the horizon.

questions.question: What helps you be seen at an intersection?

options.text: Try to make eye contact with other drivers.
Ride with your headlight on.
Reduce your space cushion.
Ride in a weaving pattern.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride with your headlight on.
questions.explanation: Keep your headlight on and ride in a lane position where oncoming traffic can see you. Keep a space cushion to escape if needed. Never assume another driver sees you, even if you make eye contact.

questions.question: What should you NOT do to prevent fatigue on a long ride?

options.text: Dress warmly.
Limit the distance traveled in a day.
Take frequent rest breaks.
Take artificial stimulants.

questions.correctAnswerText: Take artificial stimulants.
questions.explanation: To stay safe on long rides, dress for bad weather, limit riding to about six hours a day, and take a break every two hours. Do not use artificial stimulants—when they wear off, you may become very tired.

questions.question: When someone passes you from behind, what should you do?

options.text: Move onto the shoulder.
Use the left part of your lane.
Use the center part of your lane.
Use the right part of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use the center part of your lane.
questions.explanation: The center of your lane is the safest position when being passed. If you ride on the side closest to the passing vehicle, you risk a collision. If you ride on the far side, the other driver may not pull back in time.

questions.question: When do you not need as much space between you and the vehicle ahead?

options.text: When the road is slippery.
When you cannot see past the vehicle ahead.
When weather and traffic conditions are perfect.
When traffic is heavy.

questions.correctAnswerText: When weather and traffic conditions are perfect.
questions.explanation: You need more space between you and other vehicles when conditions are not perfect. Increase your distance if the road is slippery, you cannot see ahead clearly, or traffic is heavy.

questions.question: When following a car, where should you ride in the lane?

options.text: The left part.
The center part.
The right part.
The left or right parts.

questions.correctAnswerText: The center part.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of the lane so the driver ahead can see you in their rearview mirror. Drivers check their rearview mirrors more often than their side mirrors, so this position helps them notice you.

questions.question: If you need to swerve to avoid something on the road, what is important to do?

options.text: Always brake before you swerve.
Do one action and then the other—don't do both at the same time.
Always brake after you swerve.
Swerve toward the obstacle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do one action and then the other—don't do both at the same time.
questions.explanation: If you need to brake and swerve, do them separately. Either swerve first and then brake, or brake first and then swerve. Do not do both actions at the same time.

questions.question: What happens if you forget to turn off your turn signal after turning or changing lanes?

options.text: Other drivers may pull into your path.
Others may not see your brake light.
You will have fewer crashes because others will stay away.
Others may follow you too closely.

questions.correctAnswerText: Other drivers may pull into your path.
questions.explanation: Always turn off your signal after completing a turn or lane change. If you leave it on, drivers may think you are turning again and pull into your path.

questions.question: In Pennsylvania, at what blood alcohol content (BAC) are you considered to be riding under the influence?

options.text: 0.04 percent.
0.08 percent.
0.1 percent.
0.12 percent.

questions.correctAnswerText: 0.08 percent.
questions.explanation: In Pennsylvania, a BAC of 0.08 percent or higher means you are riding under the influence. This is illegal and dangerous.

questions.question: If you must ride over an object in the road, what should you do?

options.text: Stay seated until you pass it.
Rise slightly off the seat.
Move to the side to go around it.
Grip the gas tank tightly with your knees.

questions.correctAnswerText: Rise slightly off the seat.
questions.explanation: Raise yourself slightly off the seat and put your weight on the footrests. Your knees and elbows will absorb the shock when you hit the object, and you will be less likely to be thrown from the motorcycle.

questions.question: What is the best way to help other drivers see your motorcycle?

options.text: Always ride on the left side of the lane.
Wear a white helmet.
Ride in the center of the lane.
Ride with your headlight on.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride with your headlight on.
questions.explanation: Riding with your headlight on is the most effective way to help others see you. This works even during the day.

questions.question: How can you reduce the time needed to react to a hazard?

options.text: Always ride below the speed limit.
Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
Shift into neutral when slowing down.
Pull the clutch when turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: In high-risk areas like school zones or construction zones, keep your hands ready on the clutch and both brakes. This reduces your reaction time if a hazard appears.

questions.question: When riding in a group, where should inexperienced riders position themselves?

options.text: Just behind the leader.
In the front of the group.
At the back of the group.
Next to the leader.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This keeps them from falling behind, and it lets experienced riders watch them from the back of the group.
